articles.title: 114 Rafale deal likely by FY-end; French firm agrees to integrate Indian weapons: Def secy
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: In good news for the Indian Air Force, defence secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh said on Thursday that the govt is planning to conclude the contract
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In good news for the Indian Air Force, defence secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh said on Thursday that the govt is planning to conclude the contract for 114 Rafale jets by the end of this financial year and the govt is looking for a higher level of integration of Indian armaments in such 4-5-generation fighter jets.Confirming that bids submitted under the request for proposal (RFP) stage are undergoing formal assessment, the defence secretary said, “We should be able to reach some conclusion in that procurement cycle before the end of this year.”“They had agreed to integrate Indian weapons even in the already-contracted Rafale Marines that we had bought. In this case, of course, we are going one step ahead, in the sense that it's a buy-and-make programme, with the bulk of the aircraft to be assembled in India, with significant levels of indigenisation and integration of Indian systems and weapons,” Singh, who is also DRDO chairman, told ANI. India had contracted 26 Rafale Marine jets from France for Rs 63,000 crore in April 2025 for the Indian Navy.On the fifth-generation fighter jet AMCA programme, Singh said it has reached a stage where requests for proposals (RFP) have been invited from shortlisted vendors. “We haven't taken a decision to go in for any global or outside fifth-generation fighter aircraft programme. Our programme is AMCA. They've (vendors) sought more time because of the complexity.... We are going to give them some more time.”On the indigenous LCA Mk2 fighters, the defence secretary said, “As of now, LCA Mk2 is still on, with the first flight scheduled for the middle of next year. Let the prototypes come and let the Air Force evaluate them, and thereafter, we will see.”As India’s combat squadrons have been depleted to an alarming 29, the air force is desperately seeking to raise the strength of its advanced fighters. The IAF is therefore waiting eagerly for the induction of the 180 LCAMK1A aircraft, being manufactured by Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd under two different contracts. It is also eagerly waiting for the acquisition of 26 Rafale Marine jets and hopes for the early approval of the Indo-French contract for 114 Rafale jets.A few days ago, the defence secretary said, “HAL has 27 airframes ready, 11 engines from GE have come, and the other 16 airframes have been fitted with canopy engines and flown. GE has promised four engines per month during this year, so we will get 12 engines in the rest of the year. We will be able to induct at least one squadron of LCA MK1A at the end of the year. Only some residual issues are left. Weapon integration is almost done... With radar, there are still performance-related issues that are being tackled. HAL has promised 24 LCAs every year thereafter. We hope to get 83 LCAs and 97 jets as part of the second order by 2033.”

articles.title: Celebrity Traitors: Chaos, coffins and ‘Claudiapatra’ steal the show
articles.summary: There is paranoia, confusion and a battle to survive among the celebrities as they fight for survival.
articles.body:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the first episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

One person in particular may have dominated much of this opening episode, but Claudia Winkleman's gothic arrival still caused a stir.

Carried aloft by druids in a closed coffin, the show's host arrived in a church, to greet 21 anxious-looking celebrities.

"That was quite the nap," she said as she emerged.

"Claudiapatra!" gasped model and actress Jerry Hall - spotting similarities in both grandeur and hairstyles between Claudia and Cleopatra, the Egyptian queen.

Winkleman said at the show's press launch she loved her "iconic entrance", but admitted she'd initially wanted to hide in the castle's suit of armour.

"It's like a sort of GCSE history fantasy - it was either that or the grandfather clock," she said.

But the main talking point of this show was actor Richard E Grant, with his shocking admission.

Grant and presenter Maya Jama were selected as two of Winkleman's three traitors.

But immediately afterwards, Grant appeared to forget the entire point of the game, by gleefully blurting out to those around him he was actually a traitor.

You could have heard a pin drop after he said it. Stunned silence.

"It's an interesting angle," laughed singer James Blunt just afterwards, while comic Rob Beckett told him: "I think you've just done something that's never happened in the game - it is a bold strategy."

Grant later admitted, in footage for viewers of the show: "That may be the biggest mistake I have ever made in my life. I was so thrilled to have been chosen as a traitor that in my unguarded excitement, I said, 'Of course I'm a traitor'.

"I clearly need to defuse all the heat that's coming in my direction."

Ex-BBC journalist Amol Rajan swooped the following day, asking Grant: "What happened last night?"

But instead of sowing clever seeds of doubt, Grant said he'd been so "blatant" about wanting to be a traitor that he simply responded he was one, when he was asked.

It was an odd reply, perhaps because he was flustered.

Rajan labelled him the "Lord of Chaos", but Hall stayed loyal.

"I just don't believe Richard's a traitor, I've known him 30 years and he's my neighbour," she said.

"He says and does eccentric things, he's an amazing guy, but I think he's acting out because he's not been chosen."

Hall's loyalty could be tested though, given Alan Carr murdered Paloma Faith in series one by touching her face.

Comic and writer Miranda Hart also thinks Grant could be a faithful, but admitted she is confused.

Winkleman told the press launch she thought Grant blurted out his identity in error, because he was so thrilled to be a traitor.

"He was giddy, wasn't he? He's just laughing at what's happening. Fantastic," she said.

Ed Gamble, the host of BBC One and BBC Sounds spin-off show Uncloaked, added: "It felt like he'd been given the lead role in a film and he just had to tell everyone. It's such an insane moment."

Grant may find that no one tells him a secret ever again.

He did eventually decide to let the much more cool, calm and collected Jama take the lead in their subsequent decision making.

Meanwhile the other celebrities also proved their worth on the show, not least "hard man" Ross Kemp, the former EastEnders actor-turned documentary-maker, whose programmes have focused on gangs and the armed forces.

Having admitted how nervous he was in the pews of the church, he came into his own for the task, along with ex-army captain James Blunt.

They divided the celebrities into teams, leading them to successfully find the treasure on the pirate ship, bagging £15,000.

But Kemp quickly crumbled back in the castle, when paranoia set in.

The Last of Us and Game of Thrones star Bella Ramsey, a key player in the task, had grabbed a captain's hat from the boat. She playfully planted it on Kemp's head, marking their victory.

Little Mix's Leigh-Anne Pinnock then touched Kemp on the arm as she walked through the bar.

Clearly remembering how Carr killed off Faith early on, Kemp got understandably fearful he had been killed by a traitor.

This tickled Gamble, who said: "It is one of the funniest things I've ever seen - the moment he gets touched on the arm, having already thought Bella Ramsey putting a captain's hat on him is a murder in plain sight.

"What a variety of men live within the Ross Kemp sphere.

"He's a big hard man running that mission. And then immediately terrified of a member of Little Mix touching him on the arm. That's incredible."

We also learned that although quite a few celebrities wanted to be traitors, including Rajan and Beckett, comics James Acaster and Hart and mathematician Hannah Fry wanted to be faithfuls - Fry said she was "dripping with prefect energy".

Meanwhile YouTuber King Kenny and actress Myha'la had their own strategies.

"I have an innocent face; I want to avenge Niko [Omilana, the first to be banished in series one]. He left too early," Kenny said, while Myha'la added she wants to be perceived as "doughy-eyed, fun, and maybe a little naïve", unlike her scheming character in Industry.

Fashion is likely to be another talking point in the castle.

Beckett observed that when actress Julie Hesmondhalgh wore the shield she'd won, she looked like a "cardinal" in her long, red dress, adding: "I thought we were in the Vatican!"

True to form, Joe Lycett wore a polka-dot shorts suit with a purple feather collar.

Hall was also keen to strut her stuff, saying she wanted to stay long enough to "wear all my fabulous outfits".

Blunt deadpanned: "Well, look, if you go early, I'll wear your outfits."

But although the one-liners were flying, the show got very serious at the end, when the game's new twist dictated that Grant and Jama had to select their third traitor.

They had to choose two celebrities to meet them in person, to argue why they should stay, with the winner joining them and the loser becoming the show's first murder victim.

"They'll beg – there is a God. I'm loving it. Delicious," Grant said, grinning like a kid in a sweet shop.

Rajan and Acaster were chosen, having both put pressure on Grant over being a traitor.

"Amol is the biggest Rottweiler on me; it would take the heat off me for having been such a plonker," he admitted, while adding: "James Acaster is laser-eyed in his conviction that I am a traitor."

Despite wanting to be a faithful, Acaster argued a solid case to stay, telling Grant: "If I go tonight, the first person they're looking at is you."

Rajan then took the floor, saying: "I do think I am uniquely placed to take the heat off you. I'm here because I sniff out liars for a living.

"The faithful think I will identify the traitor by doing my job really well. If I'm on your side, I'll throw them off the scent."

Taking the episode full circle, they each laid in a coffin, just as Winkleman had, to await their fate.

"I'm "90% that nice, warm guy who's on the news, but I'm also 10% psychopath," Rajan had said earlier.

Although his Machiavellian side wasn't apparent when I sat opposite him for years at the BBC, it will be interesting to see what sort of a traitor he is - if he emerges from his coffin.

articles.title: A Massachusetts farm stayed under one family's care for a century and was cultivated for more than 200 years; a 2025 conservation purchase protected over 120 acres of farmland and forest for the future
articles.summary: More than 120 acres of historic farmland and nearby woodland in Essex, Massachusetts, have been permanently protected from commercial housing development
articles.body: More than 120 acres of historic farmland and nearby woodland in Essex, Massachusetts, have been permanently protected from commercial housing development after a major conservation deal was completed in early 2025. According to project details published by the Essex County Greenbelt Association, the regional land trust worked with local town leaders and state environmental agencies to place a permanent conservation restriction on historic Hoyt Farm, also known locally as Silver Brook Farm. The agreement ensures that the property, which has been farmed for more than two centuries and cared for by one family for 100 years, will remain used for farming, forestry and protection of natural habitat.Century of stewardship on historic soilLocated along John Wise Avenue in Essex, the property includes productive farm fields, mature forests and sensitive wetland areas. Records kept by the Essex Historical Society show that farmers have worked the land at Hoyt Farm since the early 1800s. The farm supplied food and animal feed to coastal communities in Essex County. The Hoyt family bought the property in the 1920s and began a century of direct care across four generations. During the past 100 years, family members grew crops, managed hay fields and cared for the surrounding forests. They also turned down commercial offers as property values rose across eastern Massachusetts. Family members worked with conservation groups to make sure future changes in ownership would not lead to subdivision or suburban development. According to official statements on the Greenbelt success story portal, protecting the farm keeps an important connection to Essex County's farming history. It also protects working farmland in an area where agricultural properties are quickly disappearing.Funding and municipal collaborationProtecting the land required several sources of funding. The money came from local government funds, state grants and private donations collected through community outreach. According to financial information released by Essex County Greenbelt, voters at an Essex Town Meeting approved a major contribution from local Community Preservation Act funds to help support the purchase. The town's contribution was then matched by grants from the Massachusetts Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs through its Agricultural Preservation Restriction program. Private donors from Essex and nearby towns provided the rest of the money needed to complete the land purchase. By combining local tax funds, state conservation grants and donations from residents, organizers completed the deal without creating an unexpected financial burden for town operations. Under the agreement, the property remains privately owned and managed. Essex County Greenbelt holds and enforces the permanent conservation restriction. This means industrial development, residential subdivisions and commercial construction are permanently banned on the property.Environmental benefits for the watershedThe protection of the 120-acre property also safeguards important natural resources and wildlife areas connected to the Essex River watershed. According to environmental assessments by Greenbelt conservation specialists, the property includes sensitive wetlands, headwater streams and forested buffer areas that drain into local salt marshes. Uncontrolled housing development could have added roads, driveways and roofs that do not absorb water. This could increase stormwater runoff and carry pollution into nearby shellfish beds. Keeping the forest and open land undisturbed allows the soil to absorb rain naturally. This helps filter water before it reaches coastal ecosystems. Environmental scientists at the Massachusetts Division of Ecological Restoration say coastal wetlands and nearby forest buffers are important for reducing local flooding during severe weather. The protected property also provides an important path for wildlife. It connects existing protected land in Essex with larger forest areas across northern Essex County.Securing agricultural land for future generationsThe protection of Hoyt Farm comes at an important time for farms across Massachusetts. Data from the United States Department of Agriculture's Census of Agriculture shows that Massachusetts lost thousands of acres of active farmland over the past two decades. Rising land prices and demand for housing have contributed to this loss. High property costs also make it difficult for young and beginning farmers to buy suitable farmland. By placing a permanent conservation restriction on the property, its commercial value falls to reflect its protected agricultural use. This can make the land more affordable for future farmers who want to work it. According to statements from Greenbelt project organizers, keeping Hoyt Farm permanently dedicated to agriculture supports local food security and protects the farming character of Essex. It also helps ensure that more than 200 years of farming history on John Wise Avenue can continue into the future.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Yes, you can use red light therapy devices on your dog — but do they actually have benefits?
articles.summary: Red light therapy can help reduce joint pain and inflammation and help heal injuries. I asked vets about how to safely use a red light therapy device on your pet.
articles.body: Red light therapy has many benefits: It can help clear acne, reduce wrinkles and even serve as a recovery tool post-workout by reducing muscle fatigue, joint pain and soreness. But what if you wanted to extend some of those benefits to your pet? After all, most pet owners will try anything to help their furry friends live longer and more comfortably. When it comes to dogs, especially senior dogs, experts say red light therapy can be useful for relieving arthritis pain and inflammation. But how exactly does it work, and is it safe for all dogs? I spoke with veterinarians about the benefits of red light therapy for dogs and how to use a device on your pet. I also rounded up the best products to consider based on my experts’ guidance, as well as options NBC Selected editors tested on their own dogs. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. Is red light therapy safe for dogs? Red light therapy is generally safe for dogs, but using it incorrectly can lead to side effects. “The biggest practical risks with higher-powered devices are eye injury and thermal burns,” says Dr. Kate Elden, veterinarian and chief medical officer at Dutch, a pet telehealth company. “Across all the recent trials for arthritis, ear infections and skin issues, we almost never see adverse events reported.” While red light therapy is usually low-risk when used correctly, that doesn’t mean it’s right for every dog. You should always talk to your veterinarian first, especially if your dog has active tumors (red light can stimulate cell growth and may speed up the growth of cancer cells, says Elden), active bleeding (can prevent clotting, which increases blood loss), reduced skin sensation (may cause nerve damage or injuries if they can’t feel the device getting too warm) or is pregnant (due to lack of safety data), says Dr. Lindsay Kendrick, the medical director at VEG ER for Pets in Boston. Best red light therapy devices for dogs If you got the green light to try red light therapy on your fur baby, consider one of the devices below. (Note: consult with your vet about whether it’s a good fit before you purchase.) Each product below has a minimum four-star average rating from 100 or more customers and/or was directly recommended by NBC Selected staffers. Best wearable device Capillus, which has provided red light therapy devices for a decade, recently expanded into pet wellness earlier this month. This vest has two rechargeable pads that cover your dog’s back, chest and stomach. It’s also fully adjustable (it has a harness-style design with adjustable buckle straps) and cordless, so you won’t have to worry about your pet getting overly uncomfortable. It has both red light and near-infrared light, which helps reach your pet’s skin and joints and deeper into the tissue. You can change the intensity of the light using a button on each pad, and the vest has a 20-minute timer that automatically turns it off when the time is up. It comes in a medium and large size. I tried this vest on my 8-year-old, 16-pound Havanese and bichon frise mix Bella, and I was surprised at how easy it was to set up and put on her. Bella hates having anything on her, whether that’s her harness, a sweater or boots. Since the vest is adjustable, it was so easy to find the right fit for Bella (who is mostly fluff), and she actually left it on for the full 20 minutes without much hassle. However, the medium size is slightly big on her, so I wouldn’t recommend it for smaller dogs. Best multipurpose The Celluma Pro is a large panel that can cover your pet’s pain points and provide relief and reduced inflammation, specifically for larger areas (and bigger dogs), according to the brand. The panel is flexible, so you can turn it into whatever shape works for your pet. For example, if your dog has hip pain, you can fold it into an arch-like shape to cover both hips and legs. “I’ve never used a red light panel like this one before, so I was a bit intimidated by it and didn’t know what to expect,” says NBC Selected reporter Zoe Malin, who tested the device with her 1-year-old mutt, Mabel. When she unpacked it, Malin was pleasantly surprised at how clear and straightforward the directions were. “Because the panel is flexible, I was able to gently bend it to accommodate where my dog was sleeping or sitting. It also comes with a little stand that I attached to prop it up by her bed,” says Malin. Since Mabel only weighs eight pounds, the panel was big enough to cover most of her body. “The panel is a very easy thing to incorporate into my dog’s day, and I love knowing I’m doing something good for her health that doesn’t require much fuss,” she says. Its rechargeable battery will last between three to 15 cycles, and it weighs less than two pounds, so you can easily take it anywhere. Plus, you can use any of the three modes (aging skin, pain management and acne) on your own skin, too. The brand recommends using it for 30 minutes a day (my experts recommend five to 15 minutes for dogs), but keep in mind it does not have an automatic shut-off feature, so you may want to set a timer. Best for joints Unlike the vest, which covers multiple areas at once, Capillus’s Joint Wrap delivers red light and near-infrared light to specific areas on your dog’s body. It comes in one size that’s meant to fit larger breeds, like German shepherds and labrador retrievers, that commonly suffer from joint-related issues, according to the brand. You can wrap it around your pet’s leg and secure it with a Velcro closure to relieve joint pains and inflammation, plus it’s cordless, rechargeable and easily adjustable. It also has a 15-minute auto-off timer, so you don’t have to worry about overdoing it. Best red light therapy alternative If you’re looking for an alternative to red light therapy, or simply hoping for another therapy tool to use in conjunction with a red light device, consider this pet bed from HigherDose, one of our favorite wellness brands. It has PEMF (Pulsed Electromagnetic Field), which uses gentle, low-frequency waves and low-intensity pulses to help improve circulation, reduce inflammation and support cellular health, according to the brand. Research shows that using PEMF sessions daily helps reduce stiffness and discomfort in dogs, and similar to red light therapy, it helps heal post-surgical wounds, fractures and soft-tissue injuries. HigherDose already has a PEMF mat for humans, and just recently extended its line with a pet bed. I received the bed from the brand to try out, and Bella immediately loved it (which is surprising considering she already has three beds in our house). It comes with a remote that I use to adjust both the PEMF frequency levels (there are six levels that range from 3 to 60 Hertz) and infrared heat (which helps with stiff joints and is Bella’s favorite part). Plus, it has a machine-washable cover and comfy bolsters for her to rest her head on. It comes in two sizes: small (for cats and small dogs up to 25 pounds) and large (for medium and large dogs up to 75 pounds). How I picked the best red light therapy devices for dogs Most veterinarians I spoke to actually discourage selecting a red light therapy device on your own. “If home treatment makes sense, your veterinarian or rehabilitation specialist should recommend the device and provide clear instructions for using it safely,” says Elden. However, you can still use an at-home device if you first consult with your veterinarian and keep the following factors in mind: Wavelength: “Wavelength and power are everything. If it doesn’t list these, don’t buy it,” says Elden. Look for wavelengths between 600–700 nanometers for skin/wounds, and 780–950 nanometers for deeper tissues like joints, says Elden. Red light versus near-infrared (NIR) light: There are two types of lights to look for in a device, depending on the kind of treatment you want to provide. “Red light is generally used for tissues closer to the skin, while near-infrared light may reach somewhat deeper,” says Kendrick.Red light also appears bright red, while near-infrared light is invisible to the naked eye. Keep in mind “there is no single correct strength, distance or session length for every dog, so a veterinarian should provide a specific plan for an individual,” says Kendrick.Clear instructions: The device should tell you exactly how to safely use it, including a timer and appropriate eye-safety guidance (more on eye safety below). “Ideally the manufacturer has published data using that device or at least provides enough technical information so that you know what you’re actually delivering,” says Elden. As always, consult with your veterinarian about how to properly use the device beforehand.FDA-cleared: Look for devices that are labeled FDA-cleared, which means the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) compares the device to similar, already cleared medical devices on the market and considers it “substantially equivalent,” according to experts in our guide to red light therapy. Can red light therapy help your dog live longer? Red light therapy, usually called photobiomodulation therapy or PBMT, uses red or near-infrared light to affect how cells produce energy and communicate. Though it can’t guarantee a longer life, red light and near-infrared light may help cells function better and calm inflammation, which can help reduce pain and benefit the healing process, says Elden. “The strongest evidence we have right now is for musculoskeletal issues, specifically osteoarthritis,” says Elden. “We see dogs getting better range of motion in joints, moving around more and having less pain. It’s also showing promising results for wound healing, surgical incisions and certain skin infections.” However, the research is growing but still mixed. There are some solid, randomized controlled trials showing clear benefits for osteoarthritis and post-op pain. But a 2023 systematic review found that a lot of older studies had poor designs, small sample sizes or didn’t report their laser settings properly, which makes the results hard to trust, says Elden. The well-established benefits are limited to joint pain and wound healing, especially when used alongside other treatments like exercise and weight management. We also take steps to ensure all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and without undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. articles.title: A Milton Keynes family spent years limiting heating; 17 solar panels, a battery and heat pump now give them five years of zero energy bills
articles.summary: For Clare Naylor and her family, winter heating once meant keeping a close eye on the energy meter.
articles.body: For Clare Naylor and her family, winter heating once meant keeping a close eye on the energy meter. The Milton Keynes household used hot-water bottles, extra blankets and jumpers to make sure its heating costs stayed within budget. That has changed after their four-bedroom detached house was fitted with solar panels, a heat pump and a large battery. The retrofit has effectively turned the property into a small power station, allowing it to generate and store electricity and send surplus power back to the grid. The family can now use Octopus Energy’s Zero Bills tariff, which guarantees no energy bills for five years as long as the household stays within its agreed fair-usage limit.How the Naylors turned their home into a mini power stationThe Naylors’ home in Milton Keynes was built in the 1980s, but it has recently undergone a major energy retrofit. The property now has 17 solar panels, a heat pump, a large battery in the garage and four new radiators. Together, the equipment allows the house to produce electricity, store it and use it for heating and everyday household needs.The changes mean the home can operate under Octopus Energy’s Zero Bills tariff. The system is designed around homes that generate slightly more energy over the course of a year than they are expected to consume. Surplus electricity can then be sold back to the grid, helping to support the economics of the tariff.For the Naylor family, that means their home is no longer simply consuming energy from the grid. It can also produce and store energy, making the property function more like a small-scale energy system.Solar panels, battery and heat pump work togetherEach part of the retrofit has a different role. The solar panels generate electricity, while the battery stores energy so it can be used when required. The heat pump replaces the household’s gas boiler as the main source of heating.The property also needed four new radiators as part of the upgrade. To qualify for the Zero Bills tariff, the house cannot use gas, including for cooking, so the family had its gas boiler removed.Nigel Banks, technical director of Zero Bills at Octopus Energy, told The Guardian that properties generally need good insulation alongside solar panels, a heat pump and a battery. The aim is for the home to generate enough energy to cover its expected use, with additional electricity potentially sold to the grid.The tariff does come with conditions. The Naylor family must stay within a fair-usage limit, while charging an electric vehicle is not covered by the zero-bill promise.The family used to spend about £130 a month on energyBefore the retrofit, the Naylors were already relatively careful with their energy use. Clare Naylor told The Guardian that the household generally kept the heating at 18C, increasing it only when family members visited. During colder periods, the family relied on slippers, hot-water bottles and jumpers to stay comfortable without pushing up their bills.Their energy costs were around £130 a month. Under the new arrangement, Naylor says that money can instead go towards holidays. The difference is also changing how the family plans to use its home. Naylor said she intends to heat the house before her children return from school, something the family did not previously do because of the need to keep energy spending under control.The change comes as British households face higher energy costs. The price cap rose by 4% on 1 October 2026, while a further increase had been predicted for January.The retrofit would have cost almost £20,000The technology came without an upfront cost for the Naylors because Santander funded the retrofit as part of a project examining ways to improve the energy efficiency of existing homes. The solar panels, heat pump and battery would have cost just under £20,000 after a government grant if the family had paid for the work itself.The project also highlights one of the biggest challenges in making older homes more energy efficient, financing the upfront cost. Santander is exploring ways to help households fund retrofits, while its existing home-improvement loan would mean repayments of £389 a month over five years for a £20,000 project at an interest rate of 6.4%.Octopus Energy's Zero Bills tariff has already been used in hundreds of new-build homes since its launch five years ago. The company is now testing whether the model can work in older properties that need retrofitting, using the Naylors' home as an example.For the family, the immediate result is a home that can generate and store much of the energy it needs while avoiding energy bills under the tariff's five-year guarantee. As Naylor prepares for winter, she plans to keep the house consistently warm and, she jokes, teach her children to remember to keep the doors shut.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Ray Vetuskey, 64, marks ‘100th birthday’ of kidney his mother donated at 52 when he was 16; transplant has lasted far beyond 15-20 years, with doctors expecting it to last for life
articles.summary: For Ray Vetuskey, a kidney is more than an organ. It is a lifelong reminder of his mother.
articles.body: For Ray Vetuskey, a kidney is more than an organ. It is a lifelong reminder of his mother.Vetuskey was only 16 when kidney failure changed his life in 1978. When dialysis failed and doctors told his family that a transplant was his only remaining option, his mother, Betty, stepped forward without hesitation.Nearly five decades later, the kidney she donated is still working, and Vetuskey is celebrating what would have been his mother’s 100th birthday by honouring the extraordinary longevity of her gift.A mother’s gift that lasted decadesBetty was 52 when she donated one of her kidneys to her teenage son. Vetuskey, who is now 64 and lives in the Rochester, New York, area, remembers her as a woman who never questioned whether she should help him.“I don’t think she gave it two thoughts,” he told NBC affiliate WHEC. “Anything she could do to help her son, I think she would have done anything — which she did in my eyes.”The transplant was performed in March 1978 at University of Rochester Medicine’s Strong Memorial Hospital.Betty died in 2008, but she would have turned 100 in June. Her milestone has taken on special meaning for Vetuskey because the kidney she donated continues to function inside him.A kidney that defied the oddsThe University of Rochester says the average donated kidney survives for around 15 to 20 years. Vetuskey’s transplant has lasted far beyond that range, making him the institution’s longest-surviving kidney transplant recipient.He still returns to the hospital once a year for routine monitoring.Doctors say the transplanted kidney is functioning so well that they expect it to continue working for the rest of his life.Miklos Z. Molnar, MD, PhD, director of Transplant Medical Services at the URochester Medicine Transplant Institute, described the case as exceptionally unusual.“It’s amazing to see him thriving with a kidney that is functioning so well after 100 years,” Molnar said in a University of Rochester statement. “It is a rare situation — definitely something we don’t see every day.”He kept a promise to his motherVetuskey still remembers the emotional moments before the transplant.He and his mother were lying on separate gurneys, holding hands, when Betty began to cry. Trying to reassure her, her teenage son told her he had something important to get back to.“We were both on the gurneys, holding hands and mom was crying and [I] said, ‘Don’t worry about a thing because I got a concert to go to and I’m not going to miss it,’” he recalled.He kept his word.Just three weeks after the operation, Vetuskey attended Genesis’ concert at the Rochester Community War Memorial on March 30, 1978.He has kept the ticket stubs from that night as a memento of the life-changing period.‘She’s right by my side’Although Betty has been gone since 2008, Vetuskey says her memory remains part of his everyday life.“Every day I think of her, doesn’t a day go by,” he told WHEC. “She’s right by my side, all the time.”He has also honoured her by having a star named after her.“She’s in the national star registry for all of eternity, she’s in the heavens,” Vetuskey said.The kidney his mother donated has now been with him for almost 48 years, making it an extraordinary medical milestone - but for Vetuskey, it remains something more personal: a part of his mother that has accompanied him through nearly an entire lifetime.You use AI every day. FBS broadcasts have averaged 1.7 million viewers this season, according to Nielsen data. By comparison, NFL ratings are essentially flat through three weeks. Some networks are up slightly, while others are down slightly. The league's decision to open on a Wednesday instead of a Thursday this season has also weighed on the overall average. The reason for the decline in college football is less obvious than when sports viewership typically falls. Ratings drops are often tied to weaker matchups, political controversy, increased television competition, changes in measurement or shifts in network distribution. None of those explanations clearly apply to college football this season. Each of the first four weeks featured at least one marquee matchup: LSU vs. Clemson in Week 1, Ohio State vs. Texas in Week 2, LSU vs. Ole Miss in Week 3, and Texas vs. Tennessee in Week 4. Here are the 10 most-watched games of the 2026 season so far: The number for Ohio State vs. Texas is particularly notable. The same matchup drew 16.6 million viewers a year ago. The delay almost certainly hurt the audience, with the game drawing fewer than 6 million viewers despite Lane Kiffin making his head coaching debut at LSU. Another possible factor is the expanded College Football Playoff. The 12-team format has reduced the consequences of early-season losses. Ohio State's defeat to Texas, for example, is unlikely to significantly damage its postseason chances. At 3-1, the Buckeyes are ranked No. 5 in the nation, ahead of several undefeated teams, including Indiana, Alabama and Florida. Longtime college football fans may also point to broader changes that have altered the sport's appeal, including conference realignment and the NIL era, which some believe has diminished the traditional connection between fans and players. articles.title: Flydubai co-pilot ‘assaulted’ captain before landing: Initial Saudi probe
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia’s Interior Ministry says pilots were returned to the UAE with an Emirati security team.
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia’s Interior Ministry says that a preliminary investigation into the emergency landing of a Flydubai flight this week found that “the pilot was assaulted by his co-pilot, resulting in various injuries to both”.

the ministry said on Thursday that an initial investigation into the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was conducted by Saudi authorities with the participation of a security team from the United Arab Emirates.

It was the first comment by the ⁠Saudi government on ⁠the incident.

Flydubai flight FZ1073 was on its way from the UAE to Israel on Wednesday when a violent incident occurred that forced it to make an emergency landing at Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz international airport in Tabuk in northwestern Saudi Arabia.

Flydubai said on the day that “an altercation occurred in the flight deck”, and that crew members secured the plane and diverted it safely.

In its statement, the Saudi Interior Ministry said that, after the aircraft was cleared for emergency landing, it arrived “safely” at 9:45am local time (06:45 GMT) with 174 passengers and eight crew members on board. “All necessary care was provided.”

At about 5:40pm that day, all the passengers continued their journey on a replacement Flydubai aircraft, while the rest of the crew – besides the captain and co-pilot – returned to Dubai on another flight, it added.

The captain and co-pilot “were taken to hospital for treatment based on an assessment of their condition”.

After their condition improved and they were medically cleared, the captain and co-pilot left Saudi Arabia for Abu Dhabi on Thursday morning, accompanied by the Emirati security team, the ministry said.

Saudi Arabia “handles emergencies in line with its international and humanitarian obligations”, the ministry added, citing the readiness of its aviation and security systems to respond to exceptional cases.

Saudi Arabia’s National Transport Safety Center said its investigation team had begun work on the incident and was coordinating with authorities to determine the circumstances and collect relevant evidence.

Captain Machchhar showed ‘immense courage’

Earlier on Thursday, the UAE chief prosecutor, Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, launched an investigation into the cockpit fight on board the Flydubai flight.

Investigators will examine the circumstances and motives behind the incident, and whether it was linked to any “terrorist activity or intent” or involved prior planning or direction, Emirati state news agency WAM reported.

The captain of flight FZ1073 is an Indian national, Smit Machchhar, who was seriously injured.

Although the incident is still under investigation, his actions to apparently thwart a midair disaster have drawn praise from world leaders and those who knew him.

Machchhar was taken to hospital in Tabuk in stable condition on Wednesday, the Indian Embassy in Riyadh said.

India’s Ministry of External Affairs confirmed Machchhar was moved to Abu Dhabi for continued treatment on Thursday. India’s ambassador to the UAE paid a visit to the captain and his family was briefed on his recovery.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday called Machchhar a hero.

“In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others. His valor helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy,” Modi wrote on X.

articles.title: Supreme Court says seize vehicle, stop RC, PUC renewal if e-challans not paid
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Many vehicle owners often ignore traffic fines for years, allowing unpaid challans to pile up and eventually land in courts.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Many vehicle owners often ignore traffic fines for years, allowing unpaid challans to pile up and eventually land in courts. Supreme Court has now directed states and UTs to impound their vehicles, noting that around 47% of challans issued across the country remain unpaid.A bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and KV Viswanathan said Thursday that issuing e-challans was not sufficient and stringent action should be taken to recover fines."Let there be random checking of vehicles, and if it is found that the e-challan issued has not been abided by or honoured, necessary steps shall be taken to impound the vehicle itself," the bench said.SC said the authorities should freeze online services for vehicles with outstanding amounts. They should bar renewal of registration certificates, issuing of duplicate registration certificates, and not entertain any request to update the owner's address, it said. "The authorities shall also deny fitness certificate until all pending traffic fines are entirely cleared and further there should be blacklisting of the vehicle concerned on the Parivahan portal," SC said."This will come in the way of the person concerned if he wants to sell his vehicle. The authorities should also proceed to block ownership transfer. For multiple violations, driving licence shall be suspended from renewal, and measures shall also be taken to suspend the driving licence which may be in force. What is most important is that no centre should be permitted to issue a PUC certificate," the bench said.Expressing displeasure with authorities for not taking action, the bench said, "We want to convey something to states/UTs/authorities plainly and simply. It is not sufficient to keep issuing e-challans to the person who is alleged to have violated the provisions of the law."SC said cops could issue lakhs of e-challans, but what was being done to recover the fines was the question at hand."We are informed by the amicus... that states/UTs have to recover Rs 49,194 crore approximately towards the e-challans issued over a period of time. We are also informed that so far an amount of Rs 26,175 crore has been recovered. What we want to convey in simple words is that authorities need to work at the ground level, having regard to the ground realities," the bench said.With the case being heard for over a decade, the court decided to check the ground situation regarding implementation of its orders."We have been monitoring this litigation by now over a period of almost 14 years. This writ petition is of 2012... During this interregnum period of one year, we have issued a slew of directions for meaningful and effective implementation of various provisions of Motor Vehicles Act and Central Motor Vehicles Rules framed therein," it said, adding that if all these were going to remain on paper and not going to be implemented, then "we may have to take stern action which may not be liked by the authorities".Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Six years, hundreds of plants and one casualty - The Palm House returns
articles.summary: The Palm House at Edinburgh's Botanic Garden is finally restored and ready for the public.
articles.body:
After six years and an unprecedented botanical operation, Edinburgh's famous Palm Houses are back.

The historic glasshouses at the Royal Botanic Garden have been closed to the public for vital restoration work.

Hundreds of plants had to be temporarily moved while repairs were done on the 19th century buildings - the vast majority of them surviving the experience.

But members of the public are once again able to enjoy the redesigned space.

The shutdown had to happen because the buildings had become leaky and rusty and needed a complete overhaul.

Glass house curator Sadie Barber is delighted that, after years of disruption, the palm houses are once again being used for their intended purpose - to protect rare and and endangered plants, and to allow people to enjoy the space.

The plants were decanted to temporary homes, and then carefully moved back into the renovated space. Sadie says this has been a great achievement that wasn't without risk.

"I think whenever you move a plant and you take it out of the ground and then you stick it in a pot, it's going to suffer or it's going to get under stress.

"So there was a bit of trepidation when we picked up the biggest plants, moved them to another place, and left them there for a number of years.

"We've done really well. It feels like a huge achievement getting all these plants back in here and having them actually so well placed.

"The glasshouse team have done an enormous job, a really exceptional job of getting the plants looking like they belong.

"So it's great to see them actually thriving already."

The buildings have undergone a huge amount of work. More than five thousand panes of glass have been replaced, and the once corroding ironwork has been repaired and repainted.

Stone work has been renovated and a partition wall between the two houses has been knocked down to create a light and airy space which shows off the historic architecture and living plants.

Prof Julia Knights is the Regius Keeper of the Botanic Garden. She says they have a wide range of plants and species, many of which are endangered.

"We've got palms, conifers, ferns, begonias, all of those families, plants are hugely important in our living collection and many of them are extinct in the wild," she said.

"So what the palm houses are doing is helping to protect so many of these species, and many of them of course have medicinal properties for human health.

"So if we don't save these we are also potentially not helping to save humanity, so it's super important."

Whilst most of the plants were saved in the process of moving, there was one major casualty - the Sabal palm tree which was over 200 years old. It had grown too tall for the glass house and had to be cut down and couldn't be stored.

But some seedlings were kept, and so its legacy has not been forgotten. One of the Sabal palm's descendants is growing in its place.

David Knott, the director of horticulture at the Botanic Garden, said: "Hopefully, because we've planted it in this glass house which is a bit taller than where it was previously, hopefully it will last a bit longer than the previous one did."

He is happy to see the new one growing in place of the old giant tree.

"There was no way that we were actually going to ever be able to transplant the Sabal palm. And that was probably one of the hardest, most poignant parts of the whole process."

David Knott hopes the people of Scotland will welcome the return of the glass houses.

"For many people in Edinburgh and throughout Scotland and throughout the world, the palm houses in Edinburgh really are one of the most iconic features of the Botanic Garden here.

And we hope when we reopen, we will be able to welcome people and they'll be able to enjoy the space as it was always intended to be."

Sadie Barber says there are signs that the plants are enjoying their new home.

"You can see new growth coming out of some of those plants that are now in the ground. One thing people will notice is little new croziers coming in, coming up from the fern crowns.

"When you see that unfurling you know a plant is happy. And if you look around there's just so much life. It's been an enormous job, but a really well done job. So we are overjoyed"

The restoration keeps the palm houses looking much as they were intended, but using modern techniques and materials which should guarantee the future of these much-loved buildings.

articles.title: PFRDA eyes plan for funds to invest directly in infrastructure
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) is preparing a roadmap to allow entities regulated by it to invest directly in
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) is preparing a roadmap to allow entities regulated by it to invest directly in large infrastructure projects, beyond the current mechanism of investing through ReITS, InVITS and alternate investment funds (AIFs), chairman S Raman told TOI."A committee has been set up to look at the issue, and internal discussions are under way to evolve a mechanism where PFRDA can invest directly in such projects. It will be long, patient capital and may be possible at least five years down the line," said Raman on the sidelines of an event on NPS Diwas.Globally, Canadian pension funds are known to invest directly in big infra projects, including in India, and they hold a significant stake in such projects, including through equity. "All such modalities are being looked into," said Raman.At the event, financial services secretary Sanjay Lohiya said that as the domestic "pension kitty" grows, people are hopeful that a lot of long-term investment, particularly in infrastructure, will be provided by these pension funds."Risk, reward and the quality of investment have to be kept in mind, but govt and other stakeholders are hopeful that slowly our pension funds will be able to provide patient capital." articles.title: No uniform explanation for collegium decisions on compassionate transfers
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court collegium's decisions to transfer judges from one HC to another are explained as being meant \"for the better administration
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court collegium's decisions to transfer judges from one HC to another are explained as being meant "for the better administration of justice". But the standard reasoning does not translate into a uniform explanation, with the collegium showing unusual compassion in approving requests from some for transfer or repatriation due to difficult family situations or health issues, while maintaining aloofness from others.There are many judges in HCs who have expressed resentment at the absence of any procedure or norm for transfer of HC judges. A member of the collegium, who will go on to become CJI, has mooted framing a transparent transfer policy. He told TOI that a judge under consideration for transfer should be warned first to mend his ways and be kept under watch for some time. Only when he does not improve should he be transferred, he said.The five-member collegium on Sept 28 recommended the repatriation of Justice T Vinod Kumar from Madras HC to his parent HC in Telangana "in view of his ensuing retirement on Nov 16". Justice Kumar was transferred from Telangana HC to Madras HC in May last year by the SC collegium headed by then CJI BR Gavai.In May last year, a complaint had reached the SC alleging that Justice Kumar, heading a division bench, had kept more than 50 judgments reserved. Sitting as a single judge, he had reserved verdicts in over 170 cases since 2020. If Justice Kumar's imminent retirement was a ground for his repatriation, no such consideration was shown to Justice D Nagarjun, who was transferred from Telangana HC to Madras HC. Justice Nagarjun, a career judicial officer who was elevated as an HC judge in March 2022, was transferred to Madras HC in April 2023. As he was due to retire on Aug 14, 2024, he sent a request to the CJI on July 25, 2024, for repatriation to his parent HC in Telangana, but the collegium remained aloof to the request and allowed him to retire in Madras HC.A Punjab and Haryana HC judge represented against his transfer to another HC, citing his wife's serious illness and disability of his child. But that evoked no compassion with the collegium, which remained firm on his transfer.Justice D V Ramana, who was only 13 years old when his railway gangman father died in an accident, rose from humble backgrounds to become a judge of Andhra Pradesh HC in Aug 2022. He was transferred to Madhya Pradesh HC in Nov 2023. On his retirement in May last year, he gave vent to his frustration. He said he was asked for options and chose Karnataka HC to enable better treatment for his wife, who had a neurological disorder. But that was not heeded. articles.title: A Somerset family has grown the same broad bean since 1875; 150 years later, the heirloom has entered a national seed collection
articles.summary: A broad bean grown by the same Somerset family since 1875 has become part of a national collection of heritage vegetables.
articles.body: A broad bean grown by the same Somerset family since 1875 has become part of a national collection of heritage vegetables. Known as Grandfather Bean, the variety has been maintained by the Burge family for around 150 years, with seed passed down through generations. In 2025, it was among 11 varieties successfully added to Garden Organic’s Heritage Seed Library after being grown and assessed as part of a project to find unusual and threatened crops. Its journey from a family garden to a permanent seed collection shows how individual growers can preserve varieties that might otherwise disappear.Importance of Somerset family’s 150-year-old broad beanGarden Organic says Grandfather Bean was grown by the Burge family in Somerset for around 150 years, making it a genuine family heirloom. The organisation records that the variety was named Grandfather Bean by the donor’s father, referring to his own great-grandfather, who was born in the 1830s. The name therefore connects the seed not only to the crop itself but also to the family history surrounding it. Garden Organic included the broad bean among the varieties successfully added to its Heritage Seed Library collection at the end of 2025.The story sits within a much longer history of broad beans in Somerset. Martock History explains that the broad bean, Vicia faba, was developed in the eastern Mediterranean during Neolithic times, with early evidence of cultivation found in several parts of Europe and the Middle East. Broad beans were also grown in England from early periods, and the crop became an important food because of its hardiness.How family seed saving kept the variety goingFor the Burge family, preserving the bean depended on keeping the seed and growing it again rather than relying on commercial supplies. Garden Organic describes such family-held varieties as seeds that have been grown, enjoyed and saved by individuals, families or groups over many years. The organisation says these seeds often carry a story that can be preserved alongside the variety itself.That approach is important because many older vegetable varieties are no longer commercially available. Garden Organic’s Sowing Your Seeds project was established to identify heirloom and unusual crops being grown across the Midlands and bring suitable examples into its Heritage Seed Library. Before a variety can be accepted, the organisation researches its history and checks whether it is already commercially available. It also looks for evidence that the seed can perform reliably from one generation to the next in the Midlands.Beans and Herbs website lists numerous varieties whose histories are tied to particular families, gardeners, places or events. Its collection includes beans that have been passed between generations, brought across continents and maintained after disappearing from commercial seed catalogues. The site also records Bridgwater, a bean grown near Bridgwater in Somerset for more than 80 years, showing how closely some bean varieties can become associated with local communities.What happened when the old bean was testedAdding Grandfather Bean to the Heritage Seed Library was not simply a matter of accepting a packet of family seed. Garden Organic explains that the varieties gathered through the project were grown and tested by its horticultural team. The plants were checked for germination, strength, pests and disease, while their characteristics were measured and recorded. The aim was to establish that each successful variety was distinctive and consistent across the plants grown.The 2025 trials began with 19 varieties. 5 were rejected because of poor germination, weak growth or excessive variation. Other plants required further treatment because they were biennials and needed a second growing season. 11 varieties ultimately passed the process and were added to the permanent collection. Grandfather Bean was one of those successful additions.The new collection gives the bean a futureGarden Organic says the Heritage Seed Library conserves heritage vegetable varieties and shares them with members so they can continue to be grown. The organisation describes the newly added varieties as being at risk of extinction and says they will be protected and shared for future generations.This gives Grandfather Bean a role beyond the Burge family. For roughly a century and a half, its survival depended on one family. Its addition to a permanent collection creates another layer of protection, ensuring that the variety is no longer held only within that family history.Martock History says the local Somerset variety dates back to the medieval period and was mentioned in parish records as early as the 12th century. It was traditionally dried and used in soups, stews and other everyday foods. The variety survived because generations of growers retained seed from the plants they wanted to grow again.Grandfather Bean now joins other unusual vegetables preserved by Garden Organic, including the dwarf French bean Weller’s Blue and the historic Golden Purslane. Weller’s Blue was passed to its donor’s father by a soldier who had served in France during the Second World War, while Golden Purslane has records reaching back to the 16th century, according to Garden Organic.You use AI every day. articles.title: Michigan decision forces removal of disgraced sports doctor Larry Nassar from sex offender registry
articles.summary: Larry Nassar was removed from the Michigan Sex Offender Registry after a state Supreme Court ruling barred retroactive application of registry laws.
articles.body: Larry Nassar, the disgraced former sports physician convicted of sexually abusing hundreds of young female athletes, has been removed from the Michigan Sex Offender Registry. The development, confirmed by the Eaton County Prosecutor’s Office on Thursday, is the result of a recent Michigan Supreme Court decision regarding the state's registry laws. Nassar is one of more than 20,000 individuals whose names were recently purged from the Michigan State Police database. On September 9, the state Supreme Court ruled that 2021 amendments to Michigan's Sex Offender Registration Act cannot be applied retroactively to older crimes. As a direct result of this ruling, state police were forced to remove individuals whose criminal conduct took place prior to July 1, 2011. While Nassar was not publicly exposed, arrested or convicted until years later, his crimes technically occurred before the 2011 cutoff date. The office added that debates over the effectiveness of the registry should be left to lawmakers in the legislature, rather than decided by the judicial branch. articles.title: Kenya's young voters weigh up the choices for next year as William Ruto seeks re-election
articles.summary: A voter mobilisation campaign has registered huge numbers of young people but it is not clear who they are backing.
articles.body:
Ademba Allans is making it "cool" to vote in Kenya.

The student journalist turned civic mobiliser launched a voter registration drive on social media earlier this year, using snappy selfies infused with music and humour to target young people.

The result astonished him and many observers of Kenyan politics – by the time the registration period ended, 2.6 million new voters across the country had signed up. He is aiming to get another 2.3 million on board in the next round.

"It was the Gen Z way of doing politics," he tells me. "Fun, trendy, sexy, fashionable. Because of how we created the hype around it, people had the fear of missing out. Everybody wanted to be involved."

Gen Z, the term used to describe people born in the late 1990s and early 2000s, burst onto the scene two years ago with mass protests that forced the government to retreat on a widely unpopular tax bill. But their victory was followed by a police crackdown that killed and injured dozens of demonstrators.

Now many young Kenyans are planning to move from the street to the ballot box, angry with a political establishment they accuse of corruption and police brutality.

And they have the numbers to make a difference - more than 30% of voting-age Kenyans are younger than 35.

Polls suggest President William Ruto is looking vulnerable.

But can Gen Z convert a decentralized digital-led rebellion into organised political power?

"These youth-led movements are a wild card, in that they are unpredictable," says political analyst Tom Mboya.

"They don't require much in the way of resources and can pop up at any time. The finance bill protests were political in nature, but the movement has not been tested at an overtly political level. So if they decide to support a candidate, then he's likely to do fairly well."

One of the strengths of the digitally savvy Gen Z activists is that they have been able to mobilise outside the party structures and ethnic allegiances that anchor Kenyan politics.

Allans has been careful not to advocate a particular candidate or party – emphasising leadership rather than politicians, marshalling a new force, he says, outside traditional tribal voting blocs.

"There has never been a case where there is a bloc that is not affiliated to any person or any party. They just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created," he says.

"It's more of a swing vote because you cannot tell who we are going to vote for."

Ruto and his United Democratic Alliance (UDA) are facing strong head winds with less than a year to go before the August 2027 vote.

More than three-quarters of respondents to a survey conducted in June felt the country was moving in the wrong direction, with two-thirds saying their personal economic situation had worsened since Ruto was elected in 2022.

But analysts argue that the president does not necessarily have to be popular to win. He is a master political organiser with the resources of the state, they say.

Ruto's political rivals are also fragmented, and it is not yet clear whether they can form a united opposition to take him on.

One man who has captured the attention of many Gen Zs is Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna. He has emerged as the leader of a movement called Linda Mwananchi (Protect the Citizen), which is getting strong support from disaffected young people.

Sifuna first caught their attention when he tried to stop police from shooting at protesters who were storming parliament during the 2024 demonstrations.

'They aimed to kill' - BBC identifies security forces who shot Kenya anti-tax protesters

Now he is championing a "people-led" movement that promotes the protection of human rights and rule of law as enshrined in the constitution.

He has yet to officially declare a run for the presidency, but is already on the road rallying support. The BBC caught up with him on a recent trip to Meru county in central Kenya, a region that voted strongly for Ruto in the last election.

"Young people want us to create an environment where everybody feels that they can compete fairly," he told me before starting out on his raucous road show.

"We need to absolutely dismantle the system so that everybody has a fair chance at life, a fair chance at education, a fair chance at employment, and the opportunities to grow themselves.

"This election in 2027 is when this theory that the young people are advancing will be put to the test," he said. "Our challenge as a leadership is to ensure you have a compelling message that then encourages people to come out, let them see the vision for the new country."

Ruto also had a compelling vision for the country when he came to power in 2022.

He promised to transform the economy from the bottom up, with a focus on lifting the marginalised. His government has since introduced changes including landmark reforms that widen access to public healthcare, but many young people felt betrayed by his austerity measures and tax hikes.

"I'm here to participate in a revolution change that we want a new Kenyan youth leader who knows the common problems that are facing the young people," 23-year-old Brandon Muremi told the BBC.

I found him in a relatively quiet corner of the final stop in a hectic day of a "rolling rally" – Sifuna's convoy visited four locations, sometimes blocking traffic as he and local politicians climbed on top of their vehicles and delivered rousing speeches at ear-splitting volumes.

"We are looking for a leader who sticks to his plans, not just talking the promises that he makes," agreed Conrad Mutangili, a 19-year-old mechanical engineering student who had come out of curiosity.

"We are looking for somebody who can actually accomplish and actually bring to the people what they are talking about," he said. "Because they promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths."

"We want immediate results," said a 22-year-old computer science student, Yvonne Kileme, acknowledging that the results of government projects may be more long-term. "And one thing that we want as youths is employment, employment, employment, employment."

Ruto argues strongly that his government is delivering jobs, and says the high rate of youth unemployment is a problem that predates his presidency.

He has reached out to Gen Z with various programmes that offer grants and loans to small business and youth-led enterprises, technology hubs and digital work opportunities.

The national youth leader of Ruto's UDA, Kariuki Ngunjiri, told the BBC he was confident of winning the election with an overwhelming majority.

"The president is a listening president and he's been able to now come down to the youth, get what their concerns are, give them jobs, and that has absolutely, even for the party, given us a head start," he said.

"We are not worried about the social media buzz because we are people who actually engage the young people on real, actual, tangible development. What you see mostly on sponsored hashtags and sponsored headlines does not really concern us."

He was speaking as a senior sports official promised to expand the stadium-building programme with another venue, at a packed UDA town hall meeting in Kangema, about 100km (60 miles) north of the capital, Nairobi.

Like so many others, 23-year-old Shintah Mutahi was job hunting.

"I came to listen to what they were saying," she said, "maybe find an opportunity for a job. I think they can give me a chance, they should just be given some time to do that."

John Kiragu, a local UDA youth leader, said he understood the grievances that had driven young people to protest.

"There have been challenges," he said, "but now the government is really trying hard to consolidate the youth. The government is implementing programmes that will really uplift their lives."

Kiragu told me he was involved in a programme to deal with youth alcoholism – a real problem in this region. Many of the young men who attended the morning town hall meeting were already drunk on a cheap local liquor.

The captain of the local football team, Calvin Ware, also turned up to hear the stadium announcement. He said he had heard similar promises many times before, especially before elections, and this one was not going to influence his vote.

"We have already made our mind," he said. "The whole government should go home. We want to build a new Kenya, new youth, new people, fresh people from all over the country, and we are not basing on tribal [allegiances] or anything else. We just want a change, a change, and a change. Nothing else."

As we were speaking, we heard a loud cheer – the event had ended and people were lining up to receive cash handouts – 350 Kenyan shillings, about $3 (£2.20).

It is common practice to pay people to attend political meetings in Kenya, and politicians can use much larger sums to try and influence votes.

"More so than many other parts of the world, money talks in an election here," says political analyst Mboya. "The cost of politics is significantly higher than in other parts of the world."

Less than a year to Kenya's election, it does feel like politics might be changing, that the race could be shaped by youth disillusionment with the political establishment. But while the Gen Z movement has rejected the "old politics" based on ethnic group and money, those have been the building blocks that win elections in Kenya.

Nobody yet knows what the energy of Gen Z voters will mean at the ballot box.

articles.title: Pakistani airstrikes in Afghanistan kill 10 civilians, Kabul and UN say
articles.summary: KABUL, Afghanistan — Pakistani airstrikes on two Afghan provinces overnight killed at least 10 civilians, Afghanistan and the United Nations said Thursday, with the cross-border conflict between the two countries showing no signs of abating.
articles.body: KABUL, Afghanistan — Pakistani airstrikes on two Afghan provinces overnight killed at least 10 civilians, Afghanistan and the United Nations said Thursday, with the cross-border conflict between the two countries showing no signs of abating. Pakistan’s Ministry of Information said its strikes were against militant hideouts in two locations and that initial reports suggested 22 militants had been killed. It did not immediately comment on the reports of civilian casualties. Its claim of militants killed could not immediately be independently verified. The United Nations mission in Afghanistan confirmed that at least 10 civilians, most of them children, were killed in the strikes on the southern province of Helmand and the eastern province of Kunar. It said nine people were injured in the airstrikes. The strikes come amid repeated cross-border clashes between the two countries, while Pakistan has repeatedly carried out airstrikes inside Afghanistan since tensions between the two countries spiraled dramatically earlier this year. The two neighbors have longstanding disputes over militant activity along their border. “Civilians continue to be affected by cross-border hostilities. UNAMA reiterates its call for de-escalation, dialogue, respect for international law and prevention of further civilian harm,” the U.N. mission said in a statement. Last week, UNAMA said it had documented over 1,100 civilian deaths and injuries in Afghanistan from cross-border violence so far this year. Pakistan denies striking civilians and says it targets militants who carry out attacks inside Pakistan. Afghanistan denies harboring militants. The spokesperson for Afghanistan’s Taliban government, Zabihullah Mujahid, said the airstrikes destroyed three civilian homes. “We condemn this act and consider this an act of aggression and a crime that violates all universally accepted principles,” he said. Mohammad Hashim, a 30-year-old resident of the village that was bombed in Kunar province, said the strike occurred at around 3 a.m. “I heard a woman calling out, asking for the stones to be moved off her; she was trapped underneath,” he said. “We pulled her out, she was injured.” He said that digging through the rubble, he also found the bodies of two men and four children. Another local resident, 32-year-old Mohammad Habib, said one of those killed was a shepherd who was not affiliated with any militant or government groups. “He was a very poor and humble man. He would let his goats out in the morning without anyone even herding them, and they would go out in the morning and return home in the evening, and (Pakistan) martyred him,” he said. Pakistan’s Ministry of Information said the airstrikes were “well planned and calibrated” against militant hideouts and camps, and had “been carried out in Afghanistan with precision and accuracy.” It added that large quantities of weapons and ammunition were located in the hideouts and were destroyed. Pakistan accuses Afghanistan’s Taliban government of allowing militants, particularly the Pakistani Taliban — formally known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP — to operate from Afghan territory and carry out attacks inside Pakistan. The TTP is separate from but allied with the Afghan Taliban, who have ruled Afghanistan since seizing power in 2021. Kabul denies providing the group a safe haven and has rejected Pakistan’s accusations. “The threat to Pakistan emanates from Afghanistan,” Pakistan’s ministry said. “Our action precisely targeted the terrorist hubs.” “Maximum precautions were taken and it was ensured that no collateral damage occurs,” the statement said and added that its campaign “will continue at full pace to wipe out” the threat of militants from the country.
